snip.t: Haemorrhagic stroke – sudden neurological deficit caused by intracerebral bleeding (parenchymal haemorrhage) or subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) from rupture of a vessel.
Haemorrhagic stroke: control blood pressure, reverse anticoagulation, treat raised intracranial pressure, and refer for neurosurgery if indicated.

exam: What immediate bedside steps do you take for a patient with suspected haemorrhagic stroke? — Assess airway, breathing, circulation; obtain rapid GCS, measure BP, secure IV access, and arrange urgent CT.
How does the ICH score influence management decisions? — Higher scores predict mortality and may prompt early neurosurgical referral.
A 55‑year‑old on warfarin presents with sudden hemiparesis; INR is 3.2. What is your next action? — Reverse anticoagulation with vitamin K and PCC before imaging.
Why is nicardine preferred over nitroprusside for BP control in acute bleed? — Nicardine provides controlled titration without increasing intracranial pressure.
Distinguish CT findings of intracerebral haemorrhage versus early ischaemic stroke. — Haemorrhage appears hyperdense; early infarct is hypodense or normal.
What complications would make you consider external ventricular drainage? — Intraventricular extension causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
Explain why antiplatelet therapy is contraindicated initially in haemorrhagic stroke. — It can worsen bleeding and increase haematoma expansion.
How would malaria‑induced thrombocytopenia alter your management? — Correct platelet count with transfusion before any invasive procedure.
ai.title: Haemorrhagic Stroke
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A haemorrhagic stroke is intracranial bleeding causing acute neurological deficit. Prompt recognition, imaging, and control of bleeding are vital, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: CT scan non‑contrast is the first imaging test; shows hyperdense blood.
If CT unavailable, lumbar puncture may show xanthochromia for subarachnoid bleed.
sections.p: Bleeding into brain parenchyma or subarachnoid space that produces a sudden focal neurological deficit.

t.b: Confirms presence, location and size of bleed – hyperdense area indicates acute blood.
Detects small or posterior fossa bleeds when CT is equivocal – shows blooming artefact.
Helps when CT is negative but suspicion of subarachnoid haemorrhage remains – xanthochromia after 12 h indicates bleed.

b: GCS 13‑15: mild, 9‑12: moderate, ≤8: severe.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and the ICH score (intracerebral haemorrhage).

b: Hypertensive arteriopathy – most common in East Africa.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy – lobar bleed in older patients.
Ruptured aneurysm – subarachnoid bleed, often in younger patients.
Coagulopathy – warfarin, DOACs, severe malaria‑induced thrombocytopenia.
Infection – cerebral malaria, TB meningitis with vasculitis, HIV‑related vasculopathy.
sections.p: Identify reversible precipitants before classifying the bleed.

b: Worst‑headache of life, often with neck stiffness (subarachnoid).
Contralateral hemiparesis or sensory loss matching bleed location.
Rapid decline in GCS – watch airway.
sections.p: Sudden onset of focal deficits, headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, or seizures.
Prioritise bedside and rapid imaging; use alternatives when resources are limited.

t.b: Determines need for urgent antihypertensive therapy – target <140 mmHg systolic.
Detects anemia or thrombocytopenia that may worsen bleed.
Guides reversal of anticoagulation – INR > 1.5 needs vitamin K or PCC.

t.a: CT head (if unavailable, refer to nearest centre)

b: Increasing intracranial pressure – worsening headache, vomiting, papilledema.
Herniation signs – unilateral pupil dilation, decerebrate posturing.
Hydrocephalus from intraventricular extension – need external drainage.
sections.p: Complications develop quickly and dictate urgent actions.

b: Lower systolic BP to 130‑140 mmHg (nicardipine, labetalol) – avoids further expansion.
Reverse anticoagulation: vitamin K + PCC for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran.
Manage seizures with levetiracetam; avoid phenytoin in hepatic dysfunction.
Maintain euvolemia, treat fever, and monitor electrolytes.
sections.p: Control bleed, protect the brain, and treat underlying cause.

b: Strict BP control (<130/80 mmHg) with thiazide or calcium‑channel blocker.
Screen for aneurysms in survivors of subarachnoid bleed – consider MR angiography when feasible.
Educate on avoiding NSAIDs and herbal agents that affect coagulation.
Vaccinate against malaria and HIV, treat infections promptly.
sections.p: Long‑term risk reduction focuses on blood pressure and secondary causes.

b: Ischaemic stroke – no blood on CT, treat with antiplatelet not antihypertensive aggressive lowering.
Brain tumour bleed – slower onset, often with prior headache history.
Meningitis – fever and neck stiffness dominate, CSF analysis required.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic acute neurological decline.

b: Early CT may miss small posterior fossa bleeds – consider MRI if suspicion remains.
Normal INR does not exclude platelet dysfunction from malaria or herbal use.
Blood pressure may be normal after the bleed; still treat aggressively if recent hypertensive surge suspected.

whenToSeekHelp: New focal weakness or speech loss
Seizure onset in a previously stable patient
